extracted.intended_audience: administrative law scholars, agency lawyers, judges, and policy makers concerned with judicial review of agency rulemaking
extracted.subtask_description: Evaluative and doctrinal criteria for judicial review of agency rulemaking (the APA 'arbitrary and capricious' / hard-look doctrine) and a proposal to permit limited post hoc rationalizations by agencies. Focuses on when courts should set aside, remand, or sustain regulations and how to weigh costs of review.

rubrics_metrics.name: APA arbitrariness review (5 U.S.C. §706(2)(A))
rubrics_metrics.description: Courts must set aside agency actions found to be 'arbitrary, capricious, [or] an abuse of discretion.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The APA's text suggests open-ended 'totality of the circumstances' analysis. The Note treats 'arbitrariness review' as inclusive of both the 'arbitrary and capricious' test and the 'substantial evidence' test for practical purposes; commentators have described the standard as variably deferential and historically lenient but later strengthened into the modern hard look doctrine. See also related case law and commentary (Mead, State Farm, Overton Park).

rubrics_metrics.name: State Farm hard-look four-part test
rubrics_metrics.description: An agency rule is arbitrary and capricious if the agency has relied on factors which Congress has not intended it to consider, entirely failed to consider an important aspect of the problem, offered an explanation for its decision that runs counter to the evidence before the agency, or is so implausible that it could not be ascribed to a difference in view or the product of agency expertise.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: State Farm's language embodies both procedural and substantive dimensions of hard-look review. Courts have generally interpreted this to require agencies to provide detailed explanations of their behavior, consider viable alternatives, explain departures from past practices, and make policy choices that are reasonable on the merits.

rubrics_metrics.name: Substantial evidence standard for on-the-record factfinding
rubrics_metrics.description: For on-the-record agency factfinding, the APA requires that actions be held unlawful if 'unsupported by substantial evidence.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Although semantically distinct, the 'substantial evidence' and 'arbitrary and capricious' tests have been applied in nearly identical fashions. See Allentown Mack, Universal Camera, Bangor Hydro-Elec., and accompanying scholarly treatments; the Note therefore uses 'arbitrariness review' inclusively.

rubrics_metrics.name: Duty to consider 'significant and viable' alternatives
rubrics_metrics.description: Agencies have a duty to consider responsible alternatives to their chosen policy and to give a reasoned explanation for rejecting such alternatives, but that duty extends only to 'significant and viable' alternatives.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: City of Brookings Municipal Tel. Co. v. FCC and Farmers Union Central Exchange articulate this limitation. The Court in State Farm avoided specifying the scope, noting the alternative there (mandating airbags rather than allowing choice) fell 'within the ambit of the existing standard.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Vermont Yankee limit on procedural supplementation
rubrics_metrics.description: Courts may not impose procedural requirements on agencies in excess of those prescribed by the APA or other sources of law.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Vermont Yankee holds that while courts require reasoned decisionmaking, they cannot force agencies to adopt procedures beyond statutory requirements; this limits courts' ability to 'deossify' rulemaking by judicially adding process.

rubrics_metrics.name: Chenery rule (no post hoc rationalization)
rubrics_metrics.description: An administrative order cannot be upheld unless the grounds upon which the agency acted in exercising its powers were those upon which its action can be sustained; courts may not uphold agency action on post hoc rationales offered for the first time in litigation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Chenery (318 U.S. 80 (1943)) prevents courts from supplying a new, legally sufficient rationale that the agency did not provide at the time of decision. The Note discusses Chenery's origin, its continued application, Justice Black's dissent (warning that Chenery may enable judicial policy-making), and examples where courts nonetheless remanded despite the record arguably supporting post hoc rationales (e.g., American Textile). Bowman Transportation presents a weaker formulation limiting courts' ability to supply reasons; courts and circuits vary in applying Chenery.

rubrics_metrics.name: Proposed criterion: allow post hoc rationalization when record supports agency rationale
rubrics_metrics.description: Courts should permit agencies to supply missing rationales ex post (i.e., relax Chenery) where the existing administrative record is sufficient to support the rationale and doing so would avoid needless remand delay and ossification.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Note argues for an expanded harmless-error review in hard-look cases: rather than remanding whenever an explanation is inadequate, the court should ask whether the record can sustain the agency's post hoc rationale. Permitting post hoc rationalization would preserve the substantive core of hard-look review while reducing decision costs (delay, ossification), status-quo bias, and the incentive to regulate via informal, less-accountable mechanisms. Countervailing concerns include judicial discretion and politicization; safeguards and limited scope (e.g., only where record supports the rationale) are contemplated.

rubrics_metrics.name: Weighing decision costs versus error costs (optimization)
rubrics_metrics.description: The stringency of hard-look review should be assessed by balancing decision costs (time, delay, ossification) against error costs (welfare losses from unwise regulation), increasing review only up to the point where marginal decision costs outweigh error-cost reductions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Note frames ossification as a tradeoff: while stringent review may deter bad agency policy (reducing error costs), it also imposes large decision costs (delays, reduced rulemaking, shift to informal regulation). Because ossification effects are hard to measure, the Note examines variables qualitatively and argues Chenery revision may improve the tradeoff in many cases.

rubrics_metrics.name: Indicators of ossification and harms to consider
rubrics_metrics.description: When evaluating the desirability of hard-look stringency, consider whether review produces systematic delays, status-quo bias, reduced experimentation, and a shift from formal rulemaking to less-transparent instruments (interpretive rules, policy statements, recalls).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Empirical and anecdotal examples (Scenic Hudson, nuclear licensing delays, automotive recalls) illustrate how remands and heavy demands for record development can derail beneficial projects or push agencies to less accountable forms of regulation. The Note cites scholarship both supporting and challenging the ossification thesis and notes empirical findings (e.g., Jordan's recovery statistics) that moderate the claim.

rubrics_metrics.name: Limitation on judicial review of agency inaction (presumption against review)
rubrics_metrics.description: There is a presumption that an agency's decision not to take enforcement action (inaction) is immune from judicial review, limiting court intervention when agencies do nothing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Heckler v. Chaney is cited for the general principle that agency inaction is presumptively unreviewable, though Massachusetts v. EPA is noted as a notable departure; this asymmetry means ossification-induced inaction often escapes judicial correction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Judicial competence and politicization concerns
rubrics_metrics.description: Judges may lack the technical and scientific expertise necessary to reliably evaluate complex regulatory records, and hard-look outcomes can be significantly influenced by judges' ideological commitments.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Note cites judges (Wald, Bazelon) warning against 'technically illiterate' courts evaluating scientific evidence and empirical work (Miles & Sunstein) suggesting ideological voting affects outcomes. These concerns bear on whether courts should be enabled to supply or evaluate post hoc rationales and whether stronger explanation requirements truly reduce error costs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Harmless-error-style analysis on remand
rubrics_metrics.description: When an agency's stated rationale is inadequate, courts should consider whether the defect is harmless in light of the record (i.e., whether the record could support a sufficient rationale) before remanding.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Note argues that many remanded rules are ultimately reinstated after agencies supplement the record, often after substantial delay; empirical work (Jordan) shows agencies recover in a large share of remands and typically within about two years. A harmless-error approach would ask whether the record contains adequate support for a valid rationale, and if so, allow the regulation to stand without the full remand/litigation cycle.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sunlight/explanation requirement as signaling and accountability device
rubrics_metrics.description: Requiring agencies to provide public, reasoned explanations may discipline agencies by producing public debate and signaling the quality of decisions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Justice Brandeis's 'sunlight' metaphor and Friendly's comment that Chenery forces agencies to 're-think' questionable regulations support the view that explanation requirements provide informational/signaling value. The Note also cites Matthew Stephenson's theory that explanation requirements function as costly signals that help courts screen undesirable regulations — but it questions how much substantive informational value elaborate rationales actually convey in highly technical fields.
